sections.h2: Where your Chattanooga lot sits matters
sections.html:
Hamilton County's seat on the Tennessee River has a housing market divided between owners and a big renter base. For 2020 to 2024, 52.4 percent of homes were owner occupied and a typical owned home was valued at $283,200. Residents numbered 194,144 on July 1, 2025, a rise of 6.9 percent since April 2020.

The city covers about 142 square miles of land, so conditions change a lot between neighborhoods. Ridge houses, river-side flood areas and historic districts each raise their own buyer questions, so begin your plan with the lot's location.

Sellers who want speed usually weigh an as-is cash purchase against a conventional listing. The cash route drops repairs, showings and appraisal conditions. If the house is tidy and time is not tight, a listing could fetch more.

A historic label can restrict what a buyer is allowed to change. Ferger Place, Fort Wood and St. Elmo carry federal historic-register listings, and the city also has local historic districts including Battery Place, Glenwood, Missionary Ridge, M.L. King and Stringer's Ridge. Before you suggest to a buyer that they can renovate the exterior, ask the Land Development Office if your address is in a local district.

  • Downtown and the North Shore sit near the Tennessee Aquarium, the Walnut Street Bridge and Coolidge Park.
  • The M.L. King district runs beside the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga campus.
  • Hixson, Highland Park and Lookout Valley, also called Tiftonia, are separate communities within the city limits.
  • East of Missionary Ridge, Brainerd Road and East Brainerd Road carry traffic toward Hamilton Place.

Public schools fall under Hamilton County Schools. Confirm the school zone for an address before you quote it to a buyer.

Buyers' inspectors check roof condition, tree cover and drainage, and a seller who fixed those items in advance gets a cleaner negotiation. Hilly lots bring their own checks, and you can prepare a short file for them:

  • Retaining wall and drainage work, with contractor invoices.
  • Engineer letters on foundations built on sloped ground.
  • Driveway grade and access details for steep lots.

Keep that file ready so it can go out with the first offer.

A cash buyer will usually look at the same items but price them in rather than ask you to fix them. If the house has had water in the yard or basement, or damage from a storm, say so in writing early. Buyers trust a seller who explains the history, and the offer comes faster.

sections.h2: Chattanooga property tax and due dates
sections.html:
City Council sets the city rate at $1.93 for each hundred dollars of assessed value. The assessment ratio is 25 percent for homes and 40 percent for commercial parcels. County taxes are billed in addition.

Bills are sent in September and fall due October 1. Nothing extra is charged until the last day of February. From March 1, interest and penalty total 1.5 percent a month. Each March the county files delinquent prior-year taxes in Chancery Court, and after three years of delinquency a property can be sold.

The City Treasurer is at Room 100, 101 E. 11th Street, 423-643-7262. A lost bill does not excuse a late payment, so pull a copy from the city's online property tax search before closing.

sections.h2: Tax freeze for homeowners 65 and older
sections.html:
Homeowners 65 or older can apply for the city's Tax Freeze, which holds the city portion of the bill steady for one year. The combined 2025 income limit is $63,470, and the home must be the primary residence. The 2026 application deadline is April 5, 2027.

The freeze covers city taxes only. County taxes and fees such as stormwater are not frozen, and the owner has to reapply every year or the taxes revert to the current rate and value. Applicants submit proof of ownership, residency, age and income. The Senior Programs line is 423-643-7274.

Until closing day, keep the application current, since a lapse returns your city bill to the current rate and value.

sections.h2: How do I dispute a Hamilton County value?
sections.html:
An informal review with the Hamilton County Assessor of Property is the first step. Helpful evidence includes sales prices of similar properties in the immediate area within the last three years, a recent private appraisal and photos. Results are mailed.

Phone the Assessor at 423-209-7300, weekdays between 8 and 4:30, to ask when the next review window opens. Properties are reappraised every four years. When the informal review fails, the county equalization board takes appeals, reached at the same number.

If the county turns you down, the state accepts a filing through August 1 of the tax year, or 45 days after the local notice when that is later.

You can host short-term guests only with a city certificate, and the zoning rules are tight. A homestay is owner-occupied for at least 183 days a year and costs $250 to apply or renew. An absentee rental costs $500 and is allowed only in commercial zones C-C, C-R, C-MU1 and C-MU2 and form-based zones CC, CX, IX, RF, RV and SH.

Each certificate lasts one year, and the Board of Zoning Appeals cannot go past the 25 percent density cap. Applications have a 60-day life from submission, and a rezoned property cannot get an absentee certificate for 18 months. For a seller, the useful rule is that a valid certificate can be transferred to a new owner of the same address, though the occupancy type cannot change. Call the Land Development Office at 423-643-5891 with questions.

sections.h2: Filing the deed and state charges
sections.html:
Chattanooga deeds go to the county Register of Deeds in the courthouse, 625 Georgia Avenue, Room 400, phone 423-209-6560, open weekdays 8 to 4. Fees and taxes tied to a deed are collected there when it is recorded.

The title company can give you a full cost list ahead of closing. It will include the state transfer tax and, on borrowed money above the first $2,000, a mortgage tax.

Before you set a date, collect payoff letters, your latest tax notice and every owner's name as it appears on the deed. Co-owner signatures and lien payoffs cause most delays, and a cash buyer with a clean title can close much faster than a listing that depends on a lender.

faqs.q: How soon can a Chattanooga cash sale close?
faqs.a: Closing is possible within about two weeks when title is clear and any estate or lien paperwork is ready. The Hamilton County Register of Deeds files the deed after signing. Delays usually come from payoff letters and co-owner signatures.

faqs.q: What is the Chattanooga city property tax rate?
faqs.a: City tax runs $1.93 per hundred dollars of assessed value, and homes are assessed at 25 percent of appraisal. The county rate is separate; the Trustee at 423-209-7270 has it.

faqs.q: Who pays the state transfer tax in a Chattanooga sale?
faqs.a: Collected at recording, the state charge is 37 cents per $100 of price. The contract decides who pays it, and the closing statement shows the amount.

faqs.q: Does a vacation rental certificate pass to a buyer?
faqs.a: Yes. It can move to the new owner of the same property when the buyer files the transfer application. It cannot follow the operator to a different address, and the occupancy type stays the same.

faqs.q: When does Hamilton County reappraise next?
faqs.a: Properties are reappraised every four years. Call the Hamilton County Assessor at 423-209-7300 for the next effective date.
